title: Read a partner's stock feed in the charset it declares

blocks.text: Partners send the stock service a nightly feed, one `name;quantity` record per line, over a connection that delivers the bytes in whatever pieces the network produces. Each partner declares the charset of its feed in its contract: most use UTF-8, two older ones Latin-1. A record with a broken name must not reach the stock tables: last month a partner switched to Latin-1 without saying so, and a week of town names was stored with `�` in them before anyone noticed.

Finish `forEachLine` in `src/main/java/practice/FeedLines.java`. It hands each line of the feed to the consumer, in order, decoded in the charset passed in, and returns how many lines there were. Bytes that aren't valid in that charset end the read with an `IOException`. Leave the stream open: the caller closes it. About five lines in total.

cases.says: each line of an ASCII feed is handed on in order, and the count is returned
a UTF-8 feed with accented names that arrives in one read is handed on intact
a Latin-1 feed is decoded with Latin-1, the charset passed in, whatever the machine's default
a multi-byte character whose bytes arrive in two different reads is decoded whole
bytes that are malformed in the declared charset end the read with a CharacterCodingException before any line is handed on

origin.section: InputStreamReader Adapts Bytes to Chars Through a Charset, and the One-Argument Constructor Takes the JVM's Default

concepts: InputStreamReader built with a Charset replaces malformed input with U+FFFD; built with a decoder from newDecoder() it throws MalformedInputException.
InputStreamReader without a charset decodes with the JVM's default charset, which a start option can change, so the same bytes read correctly on one machine and garbled, without an error, on another.
InputStreamReader keeps the bytes of an unfinished character until the next read completes it; decoding each read on its own turns a split multi-byte character into replacement characters.
